This assignment includes many interpretations of statistical tests. Please carefully read the provided statements in the solution after it posts so that you can better understand the language that statisticians use to talk about hypothesis testing. 

Be sure to run the following code chunk before continuing with the assignment.  

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(stat1080r)
```

We are going to use the `colleges` dataset from the `stat1080r` package for this assignment. Run the following code to make that dataset available in your environment. 

```{r}
colleges <- stat1080r::colleges
```

This dataset contains 831 American colleges that: 

- Offer four-year degree programs
- Have more than 2,000 students
- Have endowments larger than \$10 million

We are going to call this group the population of "large four-year schools". Note that this population does NOT represent ALL schools of higher education in the United States, but rather the "population of interest". We wish to explore the proportion of "public" schools within this population.  

# Problem 

Rarely do we have access to all the observations in our population. Normally, we must take a much smaller sample of observations to get insight into our population. However, in this case, we are able to calculate the population parameter of interest (which we will call $p$) by calculating the proportion of public schools in the dataset: 

```{r}
pop_p <- colleges |>
  summarize(mean_public = mean(public)) |>
  pull(mean_public) |>
  round(2)

pop_p
```

Now suppose that we didn't have access to the entire population of schools, which means that we do not know that `pop_p = 0.62`. Suppose instead that we only had access to one random sample of 50 schools. 

```{r}
set.seed(70211) # set seed for reproducibility
college_samp <- colleges |>
  slice_sample(n = 50)
```

Using this sample of schools, calculate a 95% confidence interval for the true proportion of public schools in our sample. Remember that you will need the following elements: 

- Your sample proportion estimate (remember that we do not know $p$)
- Your sample standard error (remember to use $\bar{X}$ instead of $p$ since we assume that $p$ is not known). 
- Your z-score, which should be equal to `qnorm(0.975)` for a 95% confidence interval. Remember that multiplying your z-score by the standard error calculates the margin of error.

# Problem 

The following code calculates the p-value for same hypothesis test we just explored, except for now the sample size contains 200 schools instead of 50. The p-value is provided at the bottom of the code chunk. 

```{r}
set.seed(12345) 
college_samp_2 <- colleges |>
  slice_sample(n = 200)
x_bar_2 <- college_samp_2 |>
  summarize(mean_public = mean(public)) |>
  pull(mean_public)
se_bar_2 <- sqrt(x_bar_2 * (1 - x_bar_2) / 200)

z_score <- (x_bar_2 - 0.5) / se_bar_2

2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z_score)))
```

Based on the p-value, what would you conclude about the hypothesis with the new sample size?
